Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:1: First we must explain the nature of fear [of Heaven], and afterward the things by which a person comes to acquire this fear in his heart. This is the fear we were commanded regarding several times in the Torah (Deuteronomy 11:11-13): "and now, Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you, but to fear the LORD your God," and likewise (ibid. 11:19), "you shall fear the LORD your God," and many verses like these. The reason is: once a person knows that the world has one Creator, that He created all existing things and directs them as He wills, and that without His flow and vitality nothing could continue to exist - as it is written (Nehemiah 9:6), "and You give life to them all" - and that if, Heaven forfend, His flow were withheld from all the worlds even for a single instant, they would all cease and be as though they had never been, since all things need Him while He needs nothing from them - he is obligated to fear Him and to accept upon himself the yoke of Torah and the yoke of the commandments, like a servant who knows he has a master and patron whom he serves; for if he does not know whom he serves, [true] service cannot take root in his heart, as it is written (I Chronicles 28:9), "know the God of your father, and serve Him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:2: This fear was explained by Rashbi (Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai), peace be upon him, in Parashat Bereshit (Zohar, Bereshit 11a), in these words: "Fear is the foundation - for a person to fear his Master, because He is great and dominant, the foundation and root of all worlds, and everything before Him is accounted as nothing, as it is said (Daniel 4:32), 'and all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing' - and [the service is] to place one's will in that place which is called fear" - to the extent relevant here. These words of his, few in quantity but rich in quality, require broad explanation, and they will be explained, with God's help, according to our limited understanding, following the plain intent that emerges from his words as a whole, toward our purpose: that the essence of this fear is to fear the Cause of all causes and the Source of all sources, who is the foundation and root of all the worlds - meaning that He sustains them through His life-force, blessed be He, which flows into them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:3: This is the first commandment we were commanded in the Torah: to know that there is a God, as it is said (Exodus 20:2), "I am the LORD your God." And this commandment is the foundation of all foundations and the pillar of everything - to know that there is a First Existing Being who brought all existence into being and who sustains it all through His supernal flow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:4: Likewise, when Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, came to speak with Israel in Egypt to draw them toward divine service, he said (ibid. 6:7), "and I will take you to Me as a people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God..." And Rashbi, peace be upon him, wrote in the Pekudin printed in Parashat Va'era (Zohar II 25a) that this is the first commandment that Israel was commanded, to recognize the Holy One, blessed be He, in general terms - in these words: "The very first of all the commandments is to know the Holy One, blessed be He, in a general way - to know that there is a supreme Ruler who is the Master of the world and who created all the worlds, the heavens and the earth and all their hosts, and this is [what is meant] in general" - to the extent relevant here. And he further explained there that this is fear in a general sense, while there is also a particular fear, of which it is said (Proverbs 1:7), "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge," and the intent is the comprehension of His actions and His governance through His supernal attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:5: At the giving of the Torah, Israel longed to know and to see whom they served, and they said to Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, "we wish to see our King," as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained. And the Holy One, blessed be He, granted their request and opened before them all the worlds, so that they heard and saw the Voice saying, "I am the LORD your God." And so it is explained, in brief, in the Tikkunim (64a), in these words: "No place above or below was found where He did not speak, even among the angels, so that no other god would be found in the world speaking from the Throne - this is [the meaning of] 'I' [Anochi], and thus the letters of Anochi add up to [the numerical value of] the Throne [Kisei] - and afterward He spoke among the angels, as it is written (Exodus 20:15 [18]), 'and all the people saw the voices' - concerning which it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:20), 'for a bird of the sky will carry the sound...' For when the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to speak to the angels, His Name descended upon them in this way, [forming the letters of] the Tetragrammaton, and so on; and this is [the meaning of] 'and all the people saw the voices' - these were angels, for each [utterance] became a voice and flew through the air, and every person of Israel who said 'we will do and we will hear' had it settle in his mouth, and it taught him the whole Torah. And afterward He spoke with them from heaven and earth, as it is written (Deuteronomy 4:36), 'from the heavens He made you hear His voice, to discipline you, and on earth He showed you His great fire...' Afterward He spoke with them from the four directions, and they looked toward the east and heard the voice, and toward the west, north, and south they heard the voice, to show that He spoke to them from every place, and there was no place above or below from which He did not speak to them - to show that 'the whole earth is full of His glory,' for He bears the upper and lower worlds, and He supports what is above and below, and the throne of glory, the angels, and the souls - He bears them all, binds them all, and unifies them all, and there is none who supports Him" - to the extent relevant here. And we have omitted from this passage what is not needed for our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:6: With this we may understand the verse (Deuteronomy 4:35), "you were shown, to know, that the LORD is God; there is none else besides Him" - meaning: you were shown, for with our own eyes we saw the reality of prophecy and knew that the LORD is God - meaning the mighty God, Master and Patron of the world, and there is none else besides Him. This is what the Targum [Onkelos] explains: "for the LORD, He is God" - for [the word] "Elaha" indicates the Godhood of the Infinite One, King of kings of kings. And so it is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Pinchas (258a): "'God' testifies to His own Godhood, that there is a God and a God of gods, and He is God over all, and there is no god over Him" - to the extent relevant here. This is the plain sense of the verse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:7: Let us proceed to explain the passage in Parashat Bereshit with which we began, which said that the essence of fear is to fear one's Master because He is great and dominant, and so on. We must know what is meant by "great" and what is meant by "dominant," since these matters bear upon the subject of fear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:8: We find in our holy Torah that when it comes to attribute fear, it attributes fear to the Tetragrammaton, as it says (Deuteronomy 11:11 [12]), "what does the LORD your God ask of you, but to fear the LORD your God," and likewise (ibid. 11:19), "you shall fear the LORD your God, and Him you shall serve," and also (ibid. 28:58), "if you do not observe to do all the words of this Torah... to fear this glorious and awesome Name, the LORD your God." And it is known that He and His Name are one, as is known more clearly to those who know the secret; and since this is so, whatever is found to be attributed to the [general term] "God" indicating greatness and dominion is likewise attributed to Him, blessed be He. And we find that the Tetragrammaton is called "great," as it is said (Psalms 145:3), "great is the LORD and highly praised, and His greatness is unsearchable." And since He is called "great," it is fitting that we investigate in which respects He is called great.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:9: We find "great" used in the verses in various senses. The first is in the sense of great illumination, stature, and spirituality - such as the two great luminaries, whose greatness was in their illumination, and the proof is that afterward they are called "the greater light" and "the lesser light," which is greatness and smallness of illumination, since the moon's light was diminished. Greatness of stature - "and the priest who is great among his brethren" (Leviticus 21:10); and similarly, "the greatness that the king had conferred upon Mordechai" (Esther 10:2). Greatness of spirituality and worth - this is what David said to Saul (I Samuel 26:24), "as your soul was great [precious] this day... so let my soul be great in the eyes of the LORD" - and greatness cannot apply to the soul except in the sense of spiritual worth and importance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:10: The second [sense of] "great" is in the sense of comprehension, as in (Psalms 104:25), "this sea, great [and wide]" - for if the intent were quantity, it would have said "and wide" [alone]; rather, surely it means great in the sense of its depth, for there are places in the sea that have no bottom. And likewise King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 92:6), "how great are Your works, O LORD; Your thoughts are very deep" - meaning that in physical creation, such as the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the other great creatures, we are amazed and say "how great" - how much more exalted, in proportion, is that which cannot be grasped in its greatness and spirituality within thought, which surely has no measure. Therefore it says "Your thoughts are very deep," and wherever "very" [me'od] is said, it indicates something without measure, as is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Va'era (27a). Now, from the greatness of the creatures He created, we may rise, by many degrees, to the greatness of our Creator, the Creator of all, whose greatness our comprehension cannot fathom, without end or limit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:11: The third sense is in respect of the extension of His power and light into created things, as in (Numbers 14:17), "and now, please, let the power of the LORD be great" - and likewise "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm," as is explained in Parashat Shelach Lecha; and from this is derived (Exodus 14:31), "and Israel saw the great hand" - meaning greatness of power and capability. The fourth is greatness of kindness and mercy, as in (Numbers 14:19), "please forgive the sin of this people, according to the greatness of Your kindness," and likewise (Isaiah 54:7), "and with great mercies I will gather you." The fifth is greatness of counsel, as it is said (Jeremiah 32:19), "great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of man..."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:12: And these five aspects contained in the word "great" apply to the Cause of all causes, to His exaltedness. The first, that He is great in the sense of illumination, is an illumination without end or limit, such that all the luminaries of the entire supernal world - and certainly whatever is beneath it - are all darkness compared to Him, as is explained in the Tikkunim (135b): "The supernal crown, even though it is a primordial light, a pure light, a polished light, is dark before the Cause of causes." And it further says: "and before the Cause of causes, no light can stand; all polished lights grow dark before Him" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:13: As for the aspect of depth of comprehension, on this account He, blessed be He, is called "Without End" [Ein Sof], for there is no end to comprehending Him - unlike all created things, for every effect can, in time, come to grasp its cause; but the Cause above all, blessed be He - from the day the world was created, and not before, there has never been anyone who attained the depth of comprehending Him. And so it is explained in Parashat Vayera (Zohar 103a), on the verse (Proverbs 31:23), "her husband is known in the gates": "Come and see: the Holy One, blessed be He, is exalted in His glory, for He is hidden and concealed in the greatest sublimity, beyond anything in the world; and there has never been, from the day the world was created, anyone who could stand upon His wisdom or comprehend Him, because He is hidden and concealed and raised higher and higher, and all the upper and lower beings cannot attach themselves [to Him] until they all say, 'blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place'" - to the extent relevant here. And from the plain sense of his words there is proof for our purpose, even though this passage is deep.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:14: Likewise the extension of His light into created things - this is simple, for "the Cause above all shines within the ten sefirot of Atzilut," and so on, as is explained in the Tikkunim (3b). And likewise greatness of mercy - He is the source of mercy, "for in the light of the King's countenance is life"; and if even in the first emanated [sefirah] we deny that judgment applies to it, how much more so regarding the Cause above all causes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:15: And the matter of "great in counsel" can be understood from what is explained in Parashat Bereshit (Zohar, Bereshit 22b) concerning "let us make man" - in these words, in brief: "What is meant by what is said (Deuteronomy 32:39), 'see now that I, I am He'? Rather, this refers to the Cause of causes, the Cause above all supernal beings - for that which is called the Cause of causes is the cause of all these causes, such that not one of these causes performs any act until it takes permission from that which is above it, as we have established above regarding 'let us make man' - 'let us make' was indeed said with reference to two, for one said this to the one above it, 'let us make,' and that one above it does nothing until it takes counsel from its fellow; but that which is called the Cause of all causes, above whom there is none and below whom there is none equal to Him - as it is written (Isaiah 40:25), 'and to whom will you liken Me, that I should be equal [to him]?' - He said, 'see now that I, I am He, and there is no god with Me' from whom He takes counsel" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:16: The reason that all these matters are attributed to the Tetragrammaton more than to the other [Divine] Names is that the Name "the LORD" [Havayah] is the source and root of all the [Divine] Names, as is explained in Sabba, Parashat Mishpatim (Sabba de-Mishpatim 96a), and further in the Tikkunim, Tikkun 57, toward its end (91b-92a), where this matter is explained even more clearly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:17: And further it is explained there concerning the greatness of the Name "the LORD" [Havayah], and it is necessary to cite it for our discussion here, in these words: "There is no angel in whom the Name 'the LORD' is not found, for it is found in every place, just as the soul is found in every single limb; and because of this a person must crown the LORD in all the sefirot, in all the thrones, in all the angels, and in every limb of a person, for there is no place empty of Him, neither above nor below. The LORD is not called by the unification of the four letters alone, but by the Cause of causes who unifies them; and because He unifies the four letters within Himself, they are called, in a single unity, 'the LORD is one and His Name is one.' For this reason, the faith of Israel was placed in these four letters, and all [other] Names are attached as appellations to this Name; there is no name, from the Infinite and the Endless, greater and more dominant than this, from it and above unto the Infinite, and below unto the Endless, and all the hosts and camps fear and tremble because of Him" - to the extent relevant here. Here it is explicitly stated that all the [other] Names, even the Name "Ehyeh" which is in [the sefirah of] Keter, are an appellation for the Name "the LORD," as it says, "and all [other] Names are attached as appellations to this Name." And it then says, "there is no name... greater and more dominant than this" - here it is explicit that greatness and dominion are attributed to the Tetragrammaton more than to all the other Names.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:18: With this we may explain the verse "great is the LORD and highly praised" with which we began - meaning: "great is the LORD" - His greatness consists of the aspects mentioned, which stem from His kindness. "And highly praised" - this is according to what has been explained in this discussion, and will be explained further below, that through the Name "the LORD" all the worlds, upper and lower, were found and created; therefore each and every one praises the LORD, blessed be He, according to its comprehension of the power of "the LORD" that has spread into it. The beings of this lower world praise Him according to the limitation of their comprehension, because they are in physical creation; and the world of the celestial spheres, being finer, praises Him more; and so on from world to world - for whoever draws nearer to the King recognizes His greatness and the might of His power more fully. And the general rule is: according to the coarseness of the matter within each being, the letters "the LORD" are stamped in it, so comprehension diminishes; and according to the refinement of the matter, so comprehension increases. And this is [the meaning of] "and highly praised" - for the multitude of worlds is beyond number, and He is praised by them, each according to its comprehension. "And His greatness" - the greatness of the Name, in respect of Himself, before His greatness spreads to the lower beings, is unsearchable; and as it spreads, each one praises Him according to its comprehension in searching out His greatness, blessed be He, insofar as it has spread into it. There is more to explain on this, but we shall not lengthen further, so as not to depart from our subject.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:19: Likewise we find in the Writings that dominion is attributed to this Name, in the words of the Psalmist, peace be upon him (Psalms 22:29), "for the kingdom is the LORD's, and He rules over the nations." And likewise in Chronicles (I Chronicles 29:11), "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the might and the glory... Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom, and [You are] exalted as head over all, and the riches and the honor are from before You, and You rule over all."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:20: And the reason that dominion is attributed to Him after all the other attributes mentioned have been stated is explained by Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the passage we have cited: that the Tetragrammaton is the inner vitality that spreads through all the worlds, just as the soul spreads through the body so that there is no place empty of it; so too the LORD is "the flow of the tree," as is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar 17a), in the discourse of Elijah. And this is the matter of the dominion attributed to Him: just as the soul is what gives a person wisdom, understanding, knowledge, power, and the other qualities in a person, which are the essence of a person's dominion - for they are all effected through the soul - so too the Name "the LORD" is the one who dominates, to effect all actions, and from Him is everything, through the Cause of causes who unifies all and to whom all is bound.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:21: Further, dominion is attributed to the Tetragrammaton in another respect, in the words of the Psalmist, peace be upon him, who said (Psalms 103:20), "Bless the LORD, His angels, mighty in strength, who do His bidding..."; "bless the LORD, all His hosts, His ministers..."; "bless the LORD, all His works, in all places of His dominion." And in order to explain the meaning of his saying "in all places of His dominion," we must briefly explain these three verses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:22: This matter can be understood from what was explained at the beginning of the previous passage, which said that there is no angel in whom the Name "the LORD" is not found - that the Name "the LORD" is found in every place - and it said, "and therefore a person must crown the LORD in all the sefirot, in all the thrones, and in all the angels." We find, then, that in the world of the Throne it is "the LORD," just as it is in [the world of] Atzilut, and likewise in the world of the angels, and likewise in [the world of] Asiyah, in every single limb of a person. And the way in which "the LORD" is found in every single limb may be understood from what is explained in the Tikkunim (139b), that every limb contains the four elements. And further, as is explained there (140a), that every limb has skin, flesh, sinews, and bones, and it is explained there that upon flesh, sinews, and bones rest blessing, holiness, and unity - and these three are known to correspond to the secret of Yud-Vav [of the Tetragrammaton]; and it is further explained there that the skin is the "image of man" - malchut - within which all forms appear, and so on. Behold, [this corresponds to] the final Heh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:23: The matter that "the LORD" is found in all creatures is explained in another way in Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Bo el Paroh (42a), in these words: "All living creatures, which are the holy creatures [chayot ha-kodesh], are called by the letters of the Holy Name, as it is said (Isaiah 43:7), 'all who are called by My Name, and whom I created for My glory' - and even all created beings were created through them [these letters], and there is no creature that is not marked with this Name, in order that it be recognized who created it. And this [Yud] is the image of the head of all creatures; [the two] Heh's are the image of the five fingers of the right hand and the five of the left; the Vav is the image of the body; and therefore, 'and to whom will you liken Me, that I should be equal,' says the Holy One - there is no creature equal to Me, even though I created it in the likeness of My own letters, for I am able to erase that form and remake it as many times as I wish..." - to the extent relevant here. Here it is explicitly stated in this passage that all His creatures are stamped with the seal of His Name, blessed be He, to indicate that one Creator made them, and that He rules over them to erase their form at will, like clay in the potter's hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:24: With this introduction, let us explain the verses "bless the LORD, His angels." In the Zohar, Parashat Lech Lecha (90a), it is explained that "His angels" refers to the righteous, in these words: "Another interpretation: 'bless the LORD, His angels' - these are the righteous on earth, who are accounted before the Holy One, blessed be He, like supernal angels in the firmament, because they are 'mighty in strength,' overcoming their [evil] inclination like a mighty man overcoming his enemies, 'to hear the voice of His word' - for they merit, every day, to hear a voice from above at the time they need it" - to the extent relevant here. Now, it is known that the souls of the righteous are hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory; therefore, corresponding to the world of the Throne, from which souls come, it says "bless the LORD, His angels" - meaning that they draw forth from Him flow and blessing, for He is the source of blessing, as is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar 30b): that "the LORD" is called "Baruch" [Blessed], and "His angels" are the souls of the righteous, who were created through "the LORD," which is the seal impressed upon the Throne, as it says (Isaiah 43:7), "all who are called by My Name, and whom I created for My glory."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:25: And corresponding to the third seal, impressed upon the angels, it says, "bless the LORD, all His hosts, His ministers, who do His will" - these are the angels, who are spiritual beings above, without an evil inclination, and therefore they always do His will; and it says "bless the LORD," meaning that they draw forth flow from "the LORD," through whom they were created, as explained in the previous passages.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:26: "Bless the LORD, all His works" - this corresponds to the fourth seal, impressed upon the world of the celestial spheres, upon the twelve constellations, the seven wandering stars, and all the [other] stars, and upon all the creatures of the lower worlds - for they are all stamped with the seal of "the LORD," as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna in the passage we cited, that there is no creature that is not marked with this Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:27: And it says "in all places of His dominion," lest you say this applies only to the supernal spiritual beings, in whom "the LORD" is found - but as for the lower, physical beings, how would they bless "the LORD"? Therefore it says "in all places of His dominion," meaning that His dominion, blessed be He, is equal in all of them, in the lower beings just as in the upper ones; and therefore it says "bless the LORD, O my soul," even though the soul below is clothed in [the world of] Asiyah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:28: Further, "in all places of His dominion" - for at first glance this phrase seems superfluous, since once the entire reality of the worlds has been mentioned, it is obvious that it is all "in all places of His dominion." Rather, the point is to include what lies between one world and another, as is explained in the Talmud (Chagigah 13a), that from the earth to the firmament is a journey of five hundred years, and likewise between one firmament and the next; and in this manner, between [the world of] Asiyah and Yetzirah, and between Yetzirah and Beriah, and so on - all this is "in all places of His dominion." And this is what is explained in the Tikkunim (91b), that there is no place empty of Him, neither above nor below. This, then, is a second aspect of the dominion attributed to "the LORD": that His dominion, blessed be He, extends through all the worlds and all the creatures of the lower worlds, all of which are stamped with His seal.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:29: This is what Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Deuteronomy 4:39), "and you shall know this day, and take it to your heart, that the LORD, He is God, in the heavens above and upon the earth below; there is none else." According to the plain sense, when he says "He is God" - the meaning is that He is the mighty, dominant God who rules over everything, for every [use of the term] "God" [Elohim] connotes strength, as in "and the mighty ones [eilei] of the land." "In the heavens above" - this includes the entire reality of the upper worlds, up to the highest heights; this is [the meaning of] "above," lest one say it means only "in the heavens" alone. "And upon the earth" - this refers to what is between the heavens and the earth, and what is between one earth and another; this is [the meaning of] "and upon the earth" stated simply. "Below" - to include the six [lower] earths and all the lower creatures within them. "There is none else" - for all of them came into being through the upper and lower [levels].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:30: Now that we know this matter of the dominion attributed to "the LORD," this very dominion is to be attributed to the Cause of all causes who unifies the letters of "the LORD," just as the author of the passage attributed dominion to Him, blessed be He, in the matter of fear, saying: "fear is the foundation - to fear one's Master, because He is great and dominant, the foundation and root," and so on - meaning that His light spreads through all the worlds, as it says in the Tikkunim (3b), "and the Cause above all shines within the ten sefirot of Atzilut, and within the ten of Beriah, and shines within the ten orders of angels, and within the ten spheres of the firmament, and does not change in any place." We find, then, that His illumination, blessed be He, in each and every world, comes about through His clothing Himself in the letters of "the LORD," as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:31: And when it says "and does not change in any place" - lest one think it means merely "and does not change" alone - for "in any place" would seem, at first glance, to refer to the places already mentioned, which were stated in the passage to be the ten of Atzilut, and so on. Rather, it appears that this follows the manner of "in all places of His dominion" in the second explanation [above]. And we thus learn that even in the air of the world, the Cause of all causes is found, clothed in the letters of "the LORD," who is one with His Name; and this is the essence of the fear of which Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, spoke (Deuteronomy 28:58), "to fear this glorious and awesome Name, the LORD your God" - and he said "this" only in the manner of pointing with a finger at something present before us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:32: Now, through this we come to know the secret of "the whole earth is full of His glory," as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Bo el Paroh (42b), that this refers to the spreading forth of the supernal Godhood - in these words: "for if His light did not spread over all creatures, how would they come to recognize Him, and how would 'the whole earth is full of His glory' be fulfilled?" - to the extent relevant here. And for this reason King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 16:8), "I have set the LORD before me always" - for by considering that "the LORD" is before him, meaning that the Cause of causes who unifies all is there, this brings a person to fear, shame, and modesty, so as not to sin before the great, glorious, and awesome King who is before him - as these words will be further explained, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:33: Now that we have explained the meaning of "great and dominant," we must explain what fear results from this for a person. The matter is this: from the fact of His being great, in the manner we have explained, fear results - that a person should feel shame before His greatness, which has no limit, whether in the aspect of great illumination, as will be explained in the next chapter, or in the aspect of His being great in counsel and mighty in deed, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:34: And from His being dominant, [it follows that He exercises] providence, as I have explained; and further, that He is dominant over the two hundred and forty-eight limbs [of the body], which are stamped with His Name - so that if one sins with them, one is found, as it were, to blemish "the LORD," the "foundation and root of all worlds" (Zohar I 11b) - meaning that His providence and His flow sustain them, as it says (Nehemiah 9:6), "and You give life to them all," as explained in the passage we cited just above, "and the Cause above all shines," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:35: This is the essence of faith: to know that if, Heaven forfend, one were to imagine that there is no God in the world, then the world would have no existence at all and would not have been created; and since a world exists, with creatures within it, they must have one Creator who created them and directs them as He wills. And all created things are like a tree, which lives only from its roots; so too, all created things live only through the Cause of all causes, who is the root that sustains everything. There is more to say on this, but there is no room here to elaborate.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:36: And this aspect, too, is revealed through the Name "the LORD," for this Name is the inner vitality that spreads through all the worlds, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the passage from the Tikkunim we cited above, that "there is no angel in whom the Name 'the LORD' is not found," and so on; and even the sun is clothed in the Name "the LORD," as is explained in the Tikkunim (145a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:37: "And everything before Him is as nothing" (ibid., continuing, Zohar I 11b) - this bears on the essence of faith: that even if one were to imagine the absence of all created things, no deficiency would thereby come upon His exalted state, blessed be He, for He was called King before the world was created, as it is said (Proverbs 8:26), "while He had not yet made the earth or the open places, the LORD reigned"; and all that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory, so that they would recognize His greatness, as Ra'aya Meheimna explains. And also at the end of all things (Isaiah 34:4), "and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host shall wither... and the LORD alone shall be exalted on that day."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:38: At the time of the creation of man, our Sages, of blessed memory, said that the angels who protested against the creation of man had their finger extended among them and were burned - showing, by way of example, that they are all of no account before Him, blessed be He, to nullify them as though they had never existed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:39: From this follow two [further] aspects of fear, beyond what has been said regarding "great and dominant." The first: since a person's life comes from Him, blessed be He, as we have explained, one must feel shame before Him, blessed be He, so as not to sin with the life that He infuses within one; and one should fear, for "if He should set His heart upon Himself, and gather to Himself His spirit and His breath, all flesh would perish together" (Job 34:14-15). And so said Daniel (5:23), "and the God in whose hand is your breath, and all your ways, Him you have not glorified." By reflecting on this, a person greatly purifies his thoughts.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:40: The second: even though He has no need of created beings, nevertheless His providence watches over them for their good, as it is said (Psalms 145:9), "and His mercies are upon all His works"; and a person should say in his heart, "what recompense shall I render to my Creator, blessed be He, for all His abundant goodness toward me every day, if I should transgress His will?" Rather, it is fitting that I perform His commandments to give Him satisfaction. This matter was explained by my teacher, peace be upon him, in his interpretation of the passage concerning "and everything before Him is as nothing."
